problem: The trap says 18-4-1 means '18% W, 4% Cr and 1% V by mass, not 18 parts, 4 parts and 1 part'. A percentage is parts per hundred, so 18% W is exactly 18 parts of tungsten in 100 parts of steel. The contrast drawn is false, and a student will come away thinking percentages and parts mean different things.
fix: 18-4-1 gives the composition by mass: 18% tungsten, 4% chromium and 1% vanadium. The remaining mass is mostly iron (about 76%) plus about 0.7% carbon. Do not read the three numbers as grams, kilograms or ratio units; they are mass percentages, so a 250 g blank holds 45 g tungsten, not 18 g.

problem: 'Mist carries fluid droplets in air; it cools little' is misleading. Mist is essentially a cooling method, since the fine droplets evaporate at the cutting zone and take heat away. Its real drawbacks are poor lubrication, low heat-carrying capacity compared with flooding, and the health risk from inhaled droplets.
fix: Mist carries fine fluid droplets in an air stream. The droplets evaporate at the cutting zone, so it cools reasonably well but lubricates poorly, and the airborne droplets are a health risk that needs extraction and PPE.

problem: The table puts ceramic and CBN/diamond at the same toughness, 'Very low'. CBN is clearly tougher than ceramic and is chosen for interrupted cutting of hardened steel, where a ceramic insert would chip. Grouping CBN with diamond in one row also hides that the two behave quite differently.
fix: Give CBN its own row: hot hardness very high, toughness low to medium, wear resistance very high, cost high. Keep diamond separate as hardest but brittle and chemically unsuitable for steel.

problem: The caption says materials are ordered by hot hardness and cost, but coated carbide is placed after uncoated carbide. The coating raises wear resistance and lowers friction; it does not make the substrate keep its hardness at a higher temperature.
fix: Say the figure is ordered roughly by hot hardness, wear resistance and cost, and note that coated carbide is placed above uncoated carbide because the coating cuts friction and wear, not because the substrate is hotter-hard.

problem: 'only a few universities teach MQL, but industry uses it to cut fluid waste' is filler about syllabi sitting inside a technical description; it tells the student nothing about how MQL works in the cut.
fix: MQL sends a small, metered oil flow carried in an air jet straight to the cutting zone. It replaces the flood stream, cuts fluid waste and disposal cost, and suits high-speed cuts in a rigid machine where the chips carry most of the heat.

problem: The cross-reference 'See 5.5 for how heat becomes wear' appears twice in the same short stretch, once in the lead and once at the end of Section 2.
fix: Keep it once, at the end of Section 2, and drop it from the lead.

problem: 'loses hardness at a few hundred degrees Celsius' is too vague to be useful; a student cannot tell whether 250 °C is safe. Carbon tool steel is tempered from about 200 °C, so its working limit is well below 300 °C.
fix: Carbon tool steel loses its temper and softens above roughly 200–250 °C, so it is limited to hand tools and low cutting speeds.
